screens.title: Raycasting, Collision Callbacks & Event Handling
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Unity detects interactions without needing two objects to physically touch, and when to use each tool. We will explore raycasts and sphere casts as precise queries that answer the question ‘what is along this path?’, then move to collision and trigger callbacks which let objects react when they touch or overlap. You will see how LayerMasks and distance limits keep queries efficient, why physics code belongs in the physics update loop, and how callbacks enable event-driven communication between independent objects. A concrete example you will build is a camera-centered shooting mechanic that uses a raycast to find a target and calls a health method when hit, plus a collectible that disappears when the player enters a trigger. Along the way I’ll highlight common mistakes like missing rigidbodies, misused update methods, and expensive per-frame casts. By the end you’ll understand both the A P I surface and the practical patterns used to make interactions stable and modular in a Unity game.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Overview
Raycasting, Collision Callbacks & Event Handling
Detect objects along paths, respond to collisions and triggers, and wire lightweight event-driven interactions between GameObjects.
In this lesson

Fourth, you will implement trigger callbacks—OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit—to detect overlaps in non-physical zones like pickups or checkpoints. screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.narratorSegment: Continuing the objectives, you will combine callbacks and LayerMasks to create modular, efficient gameplay logic. We emphasize practices like caching component references to avoid expensive calls in continuous callbacks, and the role of Rigidbody presence in making callbacks fire. Finally, you will design simple event-driven communication where one object calls another's method after a collision or raycast hit. keyIdea.title: Design habits
keyIdea.text: Cache components, use LayerMasks and distance limits, and prefer event-driven calls to keep systems decoupled and performant.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Objectives — Continued
Practical considerations
  • Cache GetComponent results in Start or Awake to avoid repeated cost in Stay callbacks.
  • Mark colliders as Is Trigger for overlap-only detection; otherwise use collision callbacks.
  • At least one object must have a Rigidbody for collision/trigger callbacks to fire.
  • Place physics changes and Rigidbody.AddForce calls inside FixedUpdate for determinism.
Event-driven example
A projectile calls TakeDamage on a target when its collision occurs. The projectile does not assume how the target stores health; it simply looks for a Health-like component and calls a method if present.
Benefit: loose coupling and single responsibility.

screens.title: Raycasting: the invisible laser
screens.narratorSegment: A raycast asks a simple question: if you shoot an invisible line from a point in a direction, what does it hit first? It returns a structured hit result that includes the collider hit, the exact point of impact, and the surface normal at that point. Raycasts are ideal when you need an immediate answer about line-of-sight, shooting, or ground checks without adding physical contact. For example, a camera-centered shooter casts a ray from the camera through the center of the screen to decide whether the player hit an enemy, then reads the hit information to call a TakeDamage method on the target. A common misconception is that raycasts will report all overlapping colliders; by default they stop at the first hit. If you need multiple results, use a non-allocating method for arrays or perform multiple casts with different offsets. Another gotcha is forgetting to set a LayerMask: without it, raycasts may test against every physics layer and waste time. As a quick practice, visualize a raycast with a debug draw: draw a red segment when you hit something and a green segment when you do not. That helps you confirm direction and distance before wiring gameplay logic. What would you test first to ensure a raycast is correctly positioned and filtered?

keyIdea.title: Raycast summary
keyIdea.text: Raycasts return the first hit and metadata; use them for precise line-of-sight and implement filters to avoid unnecessary checks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Raycasting
Definition & result
A directed query returning a RaycastHit containing the collider, hit point, and surface normal.
Common uses
  • Gun fire and instant-hit weapons.
  • Ground checks for jumping and stepping.
  • Line-of-sight for AI detection.
Example
Cast from the camera center and if a hit has a TargetHealth component, call its TakeDamage method. Use Debug.DrawRay to visualize hits versus misses.
Key Takeaway

Raycasts are lightweight single-hit queries—filter and visualize them while debugging.

Code panel (visual)
// Pseudocode representation for clarity
Ray ray = Camera.main.ViewportPointToRay(new Vector3(0.5f,0.5f,0));
RaycastHit hit;
if (Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, maxDistance, layerMask)) {
  // Debug: draw red ray to hit point
  // Try to get health component and call TakeDamage
} else {
  // Debug: draw green ray to max distance
}
Misconception
Raycasts return all nearby colliders. (They return only the first hit unless you use a different query.)
Pro tip
Use LayerMask and a reasonable maxDistance to reduce cost. Use non-alloc variants when casting many rays.

screens.title: Implementing Physics.Raycast in a shooter
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a camera-centered shooting pattern that you can implement in Update. The pattern casts a ray from the camera center toward the forward direction, checks for a hit within a set distance, visualizes the result with a short debug ray, and tries to call a TakeDamage method on the hit object. Key practical checks include ensuring Camera. main is valid, exposing a LayerMask to the Inspector, and handling null components gracefully. A misconception to avoid is performing heavy physics work inside Update without filters; always restrict hits to relevant layers so your per-frame checks remain cheap. Another pitfall is assuming a collider will always contain the component you want; use GetComponent safely and cache references where repeated calls happen. In continuous shooting or many simultaneous rays, prefer Physics. SphereCastNonAlloc or pool arrays to avoid garbage collection. Finally, test visually by drawing a green ray when you miss and a red one to the hit point when you hit. That visual feedback confirms both direction and the active LayerMask configuration. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Player Shooting
Pattern overview
  1. On input, construct a ray from Camera.main through the screen center.
  2. Call Physics.Raycast with an out RaycastHit, a max distance, and a LayerMask.
  3. Draw a debug ray for hit or miss to verify direction and filters.
  4. If the RaycastHit has a target component, call TakeDamage and destroy the projectile if applicable.
Scenario
A click triggers a shooter that should only hit objects on the TargetLayer. The shooter must not penalize performance while the player looks around.
Code (visual)
// Simplified pseudocode
void Shoot() {
  Ray ray = Camera.main.ViewportPointToRay(0.5,0.5);
  if (Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, distance, shootableLayers)) {
    Debug.DrawRay(ray.origin, ray.direction * hit.distance, Color.red, 1f);
    var target = hit.collider.GetComponent<TargetHealth>();
    if (target != null) target.TakeDamage(10);
  } else {
    Debug.DrawRay(ray.origin, ray.direction * distance, Color.green, 1f);
  }
}
Check your understanding
What happens if Camera.main is null or the LayerMask includes the player layer? Test in a simple scene to confirm behavior.

screens.title: SphereCast & Overlap methods
screens.narratorSegment: Sphere casts and overlap queries extend raycasting concepts into volumes. A sphere cast sweeps a sphere along a path and reports the first collider intersected, which is useful when your projectile has width or you want leniency around small aim errors. Overlap methods, like OverlapSphere or OverlapBox, return all colliders inside a volume at a moment in time and are commonly used for area-of-effect checks or proximity triggers. Choose sphere cast when you want a swept volume between two points, and choose overlap when you need a snapshot of everything inside a region. A frequent confusion is treating sphere casts as equivalent to multiple raycasts; while they both detect objects, sphere casts consider geometry continuously along the sweep and provide a more physically accurate result for wide projectiles. For performance, Overlap queries can return many colliders—limit layers and reuse arrays when possible. As a concrete example, simulate a shotgun by using multiple cone raycasts or a small sphere cast per pellet depending on the desired hit behavior and performance budget. Which approach would you pick for a wide, slow-moving projectile versus a tight instant-hit weapon?

keyIdea.text: SphereCast sweeps a volume along a path; Overlap queries snapshot all colliders within a region—choose based on breadth and timing needs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › SphereCast & Overlap
SphereCast
Sweeps a sphere along a direction and returns the first hit. Good for simulating projectile radius or forgiving aim.
When to use
  • Wide fast-moving bullets that could otherwise miss with a line.
  • Player capsule checks when moving through narrow gaps.
Example
Use SphereCast to detect enemies near the ray path for wider projectiles; adjust radius to control spread.
OverlapSphere / OverlapBox
Return all colliders inside a defined volume at a point in time. Use for area-of-effect damage, proximity triggers, and detection zones.
Performance notes
  • Limit layers to avoid large result sets.
  • Prefer non-alloc variants and reuse arrays to avoid GC spikes.
Analogy
SphereCast is like rolling a ball along a path; Overlap checks who is inside a room when you open the door.

screens.title: Collision Callbacks (OnCollisionEnter/Stay/Exit)
screens.narratorSegment: Collision callbacks are invoked when two colliders touch and at least one of the objects has a Rigidbody. These callbacks give you a Collision object with useful data like the other collider, contact points, and relative velocity. Use OnCollisionEnter to respond once when contact begins—for example to apply a bounce force or to trigger damage. OnCollisionStay runs every physics update while contact persists; it’s useful for continuous effects such as applying damage over time when standing in a hazardous area. OnCollisionExit fires once when contact ends, which is helpful for resetting state. A common mistake is assuming callbacks will trigger when both objects lack a Rigidbody—that won’t happen. Another subtle issue is excessive GetComponent calls inside OnCollisionStay: cache references during Start or Awake if you need to access components repeatedly. As a practical example, a ball hitting a wall can calculate a reflection vector from the contact normal and apply an impulse to bounce; the Collision object provides the contact normal and contact point required for that calculation. How might you limit the logic run in Stay to reduce overhead in busy scenes?

keyIdea.title: Collision callbacks
keyIdea.text: OnCollision callbacks provide contact data and run during physics; include one Rigidbody and cache components for efficient continuous logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Collision Callbacks
What they provide
  • Other collider and GameObject reference.
  • Contact points and surface normals.
  • Relative velocity between objects.
Example: bounce
Use the first contact normal to reflect the incoming direction and apply an impulse to the Rigidbody to simulate a bounce.
Patterns
OnCollisionEnter: one-off reactions. OnCollisionStay: continuous effects. OnCollisionExit: cleanup and state reset.
Common mistake
No callbacks fire because neither object has a Rigidbody. Add a Rigidbody to one object to ensure events occur.
Key Takeaway

Collision callbacks expose contact data and run in the physics loop—use them for physical interactions and continuous effects, caching components for efficiency.

screens.title: Trigger Callbacks (OnTriggerEnter/Stay/Exit)
screens.narratorSegment: Trigger callbacks occur when colliders marked as triggers overlap with other colliders and at least one of the objects has a Rigidbody. They are ideal for detection zones where you do not want physical response, such as pickups, checkpoints, or dialogue areas. OnTriggerEnter fires once when a collider first enters the trigger and typically contains logic such as playing a collection sound, incrementing score, or destroying the collectible. OnTriggerStay runs every physics update while the other collider remains in the trigger; use it sparingly for continuous detection like slowly healing the player while in a safe zone. OnTriggerExit lets you remove buffs or stop effects when the player leaves the zone. A common pitfall is forgetting to mark the collider as Is Trigger or forgetting the Rigidbody; without a Rigidbody on one side, triggers will not fire. Another is performing heavy GetComponent calls on every TriggerStay call—cache references instead. For a concrete use case: create a Collectible object with a trigger collider and a Collect method; when the player enters the trigger and matches the required tag, call Collect and destroy the collectible. How will you confirm the player's Rigidbody and the trigger settings in the Inspector before playtesting?

keyIdea.title: Trigger callbacks
keyIdea.text: Use triggers for non-physical overlap detection like pickups and zones; ensure one object has a Rigidbody and avoid heavy work in repeated Stay calls.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Trigger Callbacks
When to use triggers
  • Collectibles that vanish when touched.
  • Area audio or dialogue triggers.
  • Checkpoints and safe zones that don't block movement.
Example
A collectible checks other.CompareTag("Player") on OnTriggerEnter and destroys itself after granting score.
Inspector checklist
  • Is Trigger is checked on the collectible collider.
  • The player has a Collider and a Rigidbody (can be kinematic).
  • Tags and layers are correctly set for your checks.
Key Takeaway

Triggers are overlap detectors. Ensure the right Rigidbody and collider settings and avoid heavy per-frame work in Stay callbacks.

screens.title: Physics Update Loop: FixedUpdate
screens.narratorSegment: FixedUpdate is the dedicated physics update loop in Unity. It runs at a fixed timestep, typically fifty times per second, and ensures physics simulations and callbacks execute deterministically regardless of frame rate. This predictability prevents jitter and missed collisions that can occur if you manipulate Rigidbodies or rely on physics data inside Update, which runs once per frame and varies with rendering load. Place Rigidbody. AddForce calls, velocity changes, and other physics-related modifications inside FixedUpdate. The physics engine calls OnCollision and OnTrigger callbacks during the physics loop, so logic that depends on those callbacks should align with FixedUpdate timing. A useful pattern is to record input in Update and apply forces in FixedUpdate; for example, read movement intent from input in Update, store it in a field, then apply that intent to the Rigidbody in FixedUpdate. A common misconception is to assume FixedUpdate's frequency matches Update; it does not. If you require smoother movement that interpolates between physics steps, enable interpolation on the Rigidbody rather than moving physics code into Update. How will you separate input reading and physics application in your player controller to preserve determinism?

keyIdea.title: FixedUpdate rule
keyIdea.text: Run physics modifications and rely on collision triggers inside FixedUpdate; read input in Update and apply forces in FixedUpdate for consistent behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › FixedUpdate
Process: Input → Apply in FixedUpdate
  1. Update: Read player input and store it in a field (e.g., moveDirection).
  2. FixedUpdate: Use the stored input to call Rigidbody.AddForce or set velocity.
  3. Physics engine resolves movement and calls collision/trigger callbacks during the same fixed step.
  4. LateUpdate/Render: visuals update to reflect the resolved physics state; enable Rigidbody interpolation for smoothness.
Misconception
Putting Rigidbody.AddForce in Update guarantees smooth movement. (It can cause inconsistent physics because Update timing varies.)
Key Takeaway

Keep physics writes in FixedUpdate and read inputs in Update. Use interpolation for rendered smoothness between physics ticks.

screens.title: Event-driven Communication via Callbacks
screens.narratorSegment: Collision and trigger callbacks are natural event sources. When a callback occurs, scripts on both involved GameObjects are invoked. This makes callbacks an easy way to design event-driven systems where objects react without keeping direct references. The typical pattern is: an event producer detects an interaction and queries the other object for a known component or interface; if the component exists, the producer calls a method such as TakeDamage or Collect. This keeps the producer ignorant of details like how the target stores health. For example, a projectile may try to get a Health component and call TakeDamage; the target implements Health in its own way and decides what to do with the damage. To make this robust, check for null components and avoid tight coupling like direct field manipulation of other GameObjects. Also, consider UnityEvents or C# events when you need multiple listeners. A common gotcha is relying on OnCollisionEnter to notify distant systems; instead, dispatch a local event or call a manager explicitly if global state must change. How could you refactor a tight coupling where a projectile manipulates an enemy's score field directly into a cleaner event-driven call?

screens.title: LayerMask & Performance Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: LayerMasks are bitmasks used to include or exclude physics layers from queries. They are essential for keeping raycasts, sphere casts, and overlap queries efficient. Without filtering, a raycast may test against many irrelevant colliders, increasing C P U cost. When you design scenes, group similar interactive objects into layers like TargetLayer, EnvironmentLayer, and PlayerLayer so you can precisely include only what matters. Another optimization is limiting maxDistance to the expected range of interaction. For repeated queries, prefer non-alloc variants and reuse arrays to avoid garbage collection spikes. A common misconception is to rely only on tags for filtering; tags are useful for identification but they are not efficient for broad physics queries. Layers are built for physics filtering. As an example, expose a public LayerMask in your shooting script and set it via the Inspector to include only TargetLayer. During profiling, if you see a high raycast cost, narrow your LayerMask and consider fewer casts per frame or coalescing multiple checks. screens.title: Common Mistakes, Safety Notes & Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Before you ship or demonstrate a prototype, run through a short checklist to avoid behavior surprises. First, verify that at least one colliding or overlapping object has a Rigidbody; without it, collision and trigger callbacks do not fire. Second, check that colliders intended as triggers have Is Trigger checked for overlap behavior. Third, place physics modifications and Rigidbody. AddForce calls inside FixedUpdate, and gather input in Update to maintain determinism. Fourth, reduce per-frame physics cost by using LayerMasks and sensible max distances; switch to non-alloc APIs and reuse arrays for frequent queries. Fifth, avoid calling GetComponent repeatedly inside OnCollisionStay or OnTriggerStay—cache components in Start or Awake. Sixth, be mindful of tag vs layer differences: tags identify objects, while layers are for filtering physics and rendering. Finally, when profiling reveals heavy raycast usage, consider spreading casts across frames or reducing their frequency, and use sphere casts selectively for wide projectiles. These checks will prevent missed callbacks, jitter, and unpredictable behavior across different machines. Which of these checks would you prioritize in a fast-moving action scene? In this lesson you will learn how Unity detects interactions without needing two objects to physically touch, and when to use each tool. We will explore raycasts and sphere casts as precise queries that answer the question ‘what is along this path?’, then move to collision and trigger callbacks which let objects react when they touch or overlap. You will see how LayerMasks and distance limits keep queries efficient, why physics code belongs in the physics update loop, and how callbacks enable event-driven communication between independent objects. A concrete example you will build is a camera-centered shooting mechanic that uses a raycast to find a target and calls a health method when hit, plus a collectible that disappears when the player enters a trigger. Along the way I’ll highlight common mistakes like missing rigidbodies, misused update methods, and expensive per-frame casts. By the end you’ll understand both the A P I surface and the practical patterns used to make interactions stable and modular in a Unity game.

These objectives map directly to practical skills you will use during development. First, you will perform raycast and sphere cast operations to detect objects along a path and gather hit details. That includes reading the hit point and the surface normal and reacting to the hit object. Second, you will learn how to filter those results with LayerMasks and distance limits so your queries stay fast and precise. Third, you will implement collision callbacks—OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit—to respond to physical contacts when a Rigidbody is involved. Fourth, you will implement trigger callbacks—OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit—to detect overlaps in non-physical zones like pickups or checkpoints. Each objective includes a short practical reason and a mnemonic to help you remember when to apply the technique. Learning Objectives means you will detect, filter, and respond to interactions using physics queries and callbacks, focusing on predictable, modular implementations.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Continuing the objectives, you will combine callbacks and LayerMasks to create modular, efficient gameplay logic. We emphasize practices like caching component references to avoid expensive calls in continuous callbacks, and the role of Rigidbody presence in making callbacks fire. You will build the habit of using LayerMasks for filtering, limiting raycast distance, and choosing the right callback type — collision for physical contact, trigger for overlap detection. Finally, you will design simple event-driven communication where one object calls another's method after a collision or raycast hit. This pattern avoids tight coupling: a projectile need not know the internal state of a target, it just requests a TakeDamage method if available. The milestone is to produce small, predictable scenes where shooting, destructible targets, and collectibles behave consistently across different frame rates.

A raycast asks a simple question: if you shoot an invisible line from a point in a direction, what does it hit first? It returns a structured hit result that includes the collider hit, the exact point of impact, and the surface normal at that point. Raycasts are ideal when you need an immediate answer about line-of-sight, shooting, or ground checks without adding physical contact. For example, a camera-centered shooter casts a ray from the camera through the center of the screen to decide whether the player hit an enemy, then reads the hit information to call a TakeDamage method on the target. A common misconception is that raycasts will report all overlapping colliders; by default they stop at the first hit. If you need multiple results, use a non-allocating method for arrays or perform multiple casts with different offsets. Another gotcha is forgetting to set a LayerMask: without it, raycasts may test against every physics layer and waste time. As a quick practice, visualize a raycast with a debug draw: draw a red segment when you hit something and a green segment when you do not. That helps you confirm direction and distance before wiring gameplay logic. What would you test first to ensure a raycast is correctly positioned and filtered?

Let's walk through a camera-centered shooting pattern that you can implement in Update. The pattern casts a ray from the camera center toward the forward direction, checks for a hit within a set distance, visualizes the result with a short debug ray, and tries to call a TakeDamage method on the hit object. Sphere casts and overlap queries extend raycasting concepts into volumes. A sphere cast sweeps a sphere along a path and reports the first collider intersected, which is useful when your projectile has width or you want leniency around small aim errors. Overlap methods, like OverlapSphere or OverlapBox, return all colliders inside a volume at a moment in time and are commonly used for area-of-effect checks or proximity triggers. Choose sphere cast when you want a swept volume between two points, and choose overlap when you need a snapshot of everything inside a region. As a concrete example, simulate a shotgun by using multiple cone raycasts or a small sphere cast per pellet depending on the desired hit behavior and performance budget. Collision callbacks are invoked when two colliders touch and at least one of the objects has a Rigidbody. These callbacks give you a Collision object with useful data like the other collider, contact points, and relative velocity. Use OnCollisionEnter to respond once when contact begins—for example to apply a bounce force or to trigger damage. Trigger callbacks occur when colliders marked as triggers overlap with other colliders and at least one of the objects has a Rigidbody. They are ideal for detection zones where you do not want physical response, such as pickups, checkpoints, or dialogue areas.
